Chris Jacobs  

stated on October 22, 2020 in campaign mailer:

“While serving as Town Supervisor, Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.”

Democrat Nate McMurray at a NY-27 debate on Oct. 21, 2020. (Robert Kirkham/Buffalo News)

By

Jill Terreri Ramos 
  

October 28, 2020

# Jacob’s charge that McMurray raised taxes on Grand Island is correct

In a rematch between Rep. Chris Jacobs, a Republican, and Democrat Nate McMurray for the 27th Congressional District seat, Jacobs says his opponent has a track record of raising taxes and a desire to do so again.

In a large postcard sent to voters, the Jacobs campaign links McMurray with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of Queens and says: “Nate McMurray Big Tax, Big Spend: An AOC Progressive Who Will Raise Taxes.”

The mailer claims that “While serving as Town Supervisor, Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.”

We were curious about McMurray’s record on Grand Island, where he served as supervisor for four years, beginning in 2016.

## Slight increases

We spoke with McMurray, who confirmed that as a member of the town board on Grand Island, he voted to slightly increase taxes. He also proposed budgets, as supervisor, with slight tax increases, he said.

During all four years of his tenure, the increases remained under the property tax cap, he said. He also said that he was one of five people on the board, where Republicans held the other four seats.

“I had no control to raise taxes myself,” he said.

Taxes increased about $27 in 2018 for a house assessed at $210,600. The tax rate for the general fund, which makes up a large amount of town spending, decreased by 3.1%, but an increase in the sewer district tax led to the increase. The 20% of residents without sewer access generally did not have an increase.

The town’s official meeting minutes of the board session with the budget vote show that McMurray voted in favor of the increase.

McMurray said he sometimes had to fight to keep the increases from getting too high during negotiations with other board members. “I’m one of five, and everybody has their pet thing.”

In the 2019 budget, adopted in late 2018, the tax levy, or the amount raised in taxes, increased by 28% on Grand Island for the sewer system fund, though overall levy increase was 2.63 percent. Rates increased only for people using the sewer system and went down for those who do not. The combined levy for the general and highway funds fell by 4%. McMurray voted in favor of this budget.

The town’s sewer system needed costly repairs, and a prior administration reached a deal with the state Department of Environmental Conservation, McMurray said. It was his administration’s obligation to fund them, he said, a statement supported by a 2017 outside auditor’s report.

The general fund tax rate was lower when he left office than it was during his first year, but that is not true of all of the funds that tax residents.

McMurray said that the mailer makes it seem like he was recklessly raising taxes as supervisor. “It’s acting like we’re willy-nilly raising taxes,” he said. “Sure, there was a moderate increase under the tax cap.”

McMurray has campaigned on his fiscal management of Grand Island, including a claim from 2018, in which he said he was a “small-town supervisor who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had.” PolitiFact rated that claim True.

## Our ruling

Jacobs said McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners while he was town supervisor on Grand Island.

McMurray said that he raised taxes slightly while he was supervisor, which is corroborated by other documents. He also said that he couldn’t do anything unilaterally, and that he was a member of a five-member board.

We rate Jacobs’ claim True.

Nate McMurray  

stated on August 8, 2018 in a news conference at the UAW 897 hall in Hamburg. :

**Says he’s a “small-town supervisor who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had.”**

Nathan McMurray

By

Jill Terreri Ramos 
  

August 29, 2018

# McMurray claims financial victories on Grand Island

As Democrat Nathan McMurray looks for votes in a Republican-leaning congressional district, he points to his record as Grand Island town supervisor the last two and a half years.

On Aug. 8, the day Republican incumbent Chris Collins was arrested on insider trading charges, McMurray held a news conference and prepared his supporters for the attacks he said will come in the race for New York’s 27th Congressional District.

“The cheaters are still going to fight,” McMurray said. “They’re still going to try to cheat. They’re going to try to label me, someone who’s been a small-town supervisor, who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had, who is an Eagle Scout, who is a father and a husband and a dad, that I’m some type of radical because I have a D next to my name. When is this game of party affiliation going to end?”

We decided to evaluate the claims he made about his tenure as Grand Island supervisor. He began a four-year term in January 2016.

## Balanced budget

Local governments must adopt balanced budgets, according to the New York State Comptroller’s Office. Excluding capital projects which are funded by debt not included in balanced budget calculations, the town took in $19.9 million in 2016 and spent $18.6 million, according to the town’s financial statements.

In 2017, the town posted revenues of $20 million and spent $19.1 million.

Deducting spending on capital projects from the town’s financial statements is the most accurate way to evaluate McMurray’s balanced budget claim, said Pam Barton, Grand Island’s accountant.

## Surpluses

Is that the same as a surplus?

The generally accepted definition of “surplus” in town government is the amount of money in “unassigned fund balance” in the town’s general fund, Barton said.

For Grand Island, the unassigned fund balance was $5.9 million in 2015, the year before McMurray took office, $6.8 million in 2016 and $6.7 million in 2017. It dropped a bit last year but was still higher than the surplus from the year before he took office.

## Credit ratings

Grand Island received its highest credit rating since at least 2001 in September 2016, Barton said.

When Barton became town accountant in 2001, the town’s bond rating was A2, she said, four notches below its current rating of Aa1 by Moody’s Investors Service.

The town’s current rating is the second-highest on Moody’s scale. Barton said because of the town’s size and budget, it likely will never reach the highest rating.

Barton said the town has always been rated by Moody’s, and has not received ratings from Standard & Poor’s or Fitch Ratings.

## Our ruling

McMurray made three claims about his record of managing Grand Island’s finances.

It’s fair to point out that Grand Island’s strong financial position is the result of years of sound management, not only changes made since McMurray took office in 2016, Barton said.

“He’s been continuing the things that have been in place from before,” the town accountant said.

Still, his claim about keeping a balanced budget is true.

McMurray’s claim about increasing surpluses is mostly true. The town had more surplus funds at the end of 2017 than it did when he took office, though it decreased slightly in his second year in office.

His claim that the town has the highest credit rating it has ever had is true, based on all available information.

We rate his statement True.

# Property owners fuming at valuation increases, assessor says changes reflect market

---

by Steve White

Tue, June 9, 2020 at 6:16 PM

Updated Fri, June 12, 2020 at 5:08 PM

3VIEW ALL PHOTOS

Kristi Wold Hall County Assessor speaks to county commissioners June 9, 2020 (NTV News)

GRAND ISLAND, Neb — Property owners are fuming at the prospect of higher taxes in a community hit hard by the virus.

"Given a 100 year pandemic that's going on. I can't believe we chose the year to do this," said Andy Marsh of Keystone Properties, which runs the Continental Gardens apartments in Grand Island.

A day after helping five tenants apply for relief funds to cover their rent, Marsh went before the Hall County Board.

He said his taxes will likely go up tens of thousands of dollars, even hundreds of thousands, which could force him to raise rent, after the county raised the valuation on his property.

"143 percent increase on one property in our organization," Marsh told NTV.

Marsh was one of several property owners to speak up Tuesday.

Hall County Assessor Kristi Wold said it's important to understand they base valuations on market conditions January First.

"Nebraska is a market state so if your neighbors are selling and buying high, unfortunately it affects you," she said following the meeting.

And while the pandemic has had an impact, homes continue to sell.

"Our house sales have not slowed at all even during COVID," Wold said.

Some county commissioners said home owners shouldn't focus on the increase, but think about what their home would sell for, and the valuation should be close.

"If you would not sell it for the price on it now, file a protest," Wold said. "We have referees in to help with those, with make appointments, it's a smooth process but you have to have evidence why your value's too high."

Other commissioners said the county needs to adapt to changing economics and find a way to provide relief.

Wold said valuations in Hall County are on the low end of what they can be, and said her office follows state guidelines.

Andy Marsh said that may be, but he thinks any increase should be done incrementally, instead of a hit when his tenants can lease afford it.

"One of our properties did not increase 3.7 million dollars in one year, and now to fix the county's problem in one year, not fair to us," he said.

Marsh said he'd have to raise rent $40-50, which could mean a decision between food and medicine or rent. Marsh said he has his finger on the pulse, as a landlord and also a board member for the Hope Harbor homeless shelter.

The county assessor says if you plan to protest it helps to have documentation or a recent appraisal. Forms are available online.

# Grand Island maintains property tax rate despite county increases

---

by Ariana Joy Cobler

Wed, September 10, 2025 at 3:26 PM

Grand Island Property Tax Revenue History

GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — Grand Island's property tax rate will remain unchanged after the city council voted to lower the mill levy for the seventh consecutive year. The budget was officially approved last night with a 9-1 vote.

According to the Internal Revenue Service mill levies are adjusted periodically to meet local budget needs, usually with public input or approval. A higher mill rate means higher property taxes. Lower property tax rates can increase demand for properties in an area.

While Hall County may be raising property taxes, the city of Grand Island has kept its property tax collections steady at approximately $12 million since 2018. This is in contrast to other Tri-Cities, where tax collections have risen by about $1.5 million since 2017.

The newly approved budget includes $24 million for parks and recreation projects. According to the city council, $16 million of tax revenue will be invested in Island Oasis, with the remainder allocated to refreshing and renewing parks throughout Grand Island.

"They want to attract more people to the city - and he says one way to do that is with the parks," said City Council Member Jason Conley.

# Commissioners 'embarrassed' to learn paperwork issue could raise taxes on rental property owners

---

by Steve White

Tue, August 1, 2023 at 7:29 PM

4VIEW ALL PHOTOS

AUGUST 1, 2023: Hall County Commissioners say they're frustrated some property owners who wanted to protest rising valuations had their paperwork dismissed. (Photo Credit: NTV News)

GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — A technicality could lead to some Grand Island renters paying more. Some rental property owners say they tried to protest higher assessed values on their properties but the paperwork was rejected.

“This is going to hurt people, to the point we don't know what will happen. It's probably going to put people in their cars and homeless,” said Karen Bredthauer, a Hall County Commissioner.

On 16 duplexes in northwest Grand Island property manager Ray O'Connor says the county lowered the assessed value on four units but on a dozen others the valuation rose $1,127,605. O’Connor said that million dollar jump likely means higher taxes.

“It's about a 24,000 hit in taxes. It's embarrassing to me,” he said of his paperwork mistake.

It’s a feeling county commissioners share after learning O'Connor protested the rising valuation but missed something on the form, so his protest doesn't count.

“Real candidly we're embarrassed it happened this way we'll try to improve procedures in the future,” County Chairman Ron Peterson said.

“I'm as embarrassed as he mentioned as well,” said fellow commissioner Pam Lancaster.

Three landlords who collectively manage hundreds of rental units came before county commissioners because of concerns.

“They will have to trickle this down to their renters,” Bredthauer said after the meeting.

She said she attended training about changes to property tax protests but didn't realize the form says if anything is missing the protest is dismissed. And in this case she says that hits renters.

“People live paycheck to paycheck. 80 percent of our population does. So when this hits them, this is food off the table, this is kids not going to games, not going to the movies, this is going to impact families, retired people on fixed incomes because of one technicality,” she said.

The deputy county assessor says they're doing what the law requires. County Assessor Kristi Wold previously told us people are paying top dollar to buy homes. Nebraska law requires valuations to consider sales when setting valuations so Wold said market forces are responsible for rising valuations.

Wold’s deputy, Mandy Pfeil told commissioners, “We did our jobs and everybody's making it seem like we're these horrible, horrible people. We just do what we have to do.”

What no one in the county did is something they may do next year and notify those who missed something in the paperwork, giving them a chance to have their protest heard.

Peterson said he doesn’t fault Wold and the assessor’s office. He said they are following guidelines.

During the meeting commissioners said protests are given to the county clerk’s office. With more than 1,700 protests this year commissioners said it would have been difficult to screen forms to see which had missing information.

With the prospect that taxes could rise Commissioner Bredthauer proposes using extra funds as tax relief. She wants to take more than $1.5 million from the county’s inheritance tax fund and use that but she said the idea doesn't seem to be gaining traction.
